inventory.query: select id, code, label, notes; order by id ascending

editorialRules: Every entry names an actual organism or an explicitly identified taxonomic group.
Scientific statements are paraphrased from museum, university, botanical-garden, or original research sources.
The final sentence of each note is an original humorous interpretation, not a biological claim.
No entry claims the app possesses preserved tissues, extracts, roadkill, or physical museum specimens.
Fungi are identified as fungi. They are not classified as plants or animals.
Source URLs are editorial evidence. Runtime UI must continue to read stored Supabase content.

publicRows.label: Gympie-gympie (Dendrocnide moroides)
publicRows.notes: This Australian stinging plant carries fine hairs that deliver potent toxins and can cause lasting pain. Soft-looking leaves; aggressively enforced personal space.
verifiedFacts: Australian Dendrocnide plants have toxin-delivering stinging hairs and can cause long-lasting pain.
The Australian Museum identifies D. moroides as the gympie or stinging bush.
removedClaims: Invented handling claim about a specific 1910 herbarium sheet.

publicRows.label: Cane toad (Rhinella marina)
publicRows.notes: This large toad was introduced to Australia in 1935 to control cane beetles. The effort failed, and the toads spread. Pest-control hire; permanent tenant.
verifiedFacts: Australian introduction occurred in 1935.
The beetle-control attempt was unsuccessful and the species spread across northern Australia.
removedClaims: Unsubstantiated roadkill condition and truck encounter.
Anthropomorphic claim that toads refused to eat beetles.

publicRows.label: Exploding ant (Colobopsis explodens)
publicRows.notes: Small workers defend the colony by rupturing their bodies and releasing sticky gland secretions, killing themselves. A security system with no reset button.
verifiedFacts: Minor workers can rupture their bodies in defense.
The secretions come from enlarged glands; the defending worker dies.
removedClaims: Imprecise claim that all internal organs rupture.

publicRows.label: Pacific razor clam (Siliqua patula)
publicRows.notes: This Pacific bivalve burrows vertically through sand and can dig roughly a foot per minute. The beach's least sociable elevator.
verifiedFacts: Pacific razor clams burrow vertically in sand.
Oregon State Sea Grant reports digging speeds up to a foot per minute.
removedClaims: Invented severed-foot preservation and formalin storage.

publicRows.label: Zombie-ant fungus (Ophiocordyceps unilateralis complex)
publicRows.notes: These fungi manipulate carpenter ants into gripping vegetation before a spore-bearing stalk grows from the dead ant's head. The final performance review has a fungal attachment.
verifiedFacts: The reported research concerns a species complex rather than one universally interchangeable fungus.
Infected carpenter ants climb vegetation and attach by their mandibles.
The fungus later produces a spore-bearing stalk from the head.
removedClaims: Unsupported assertion that the fungus hijacks motor neurons.
Uniform humidity and leaf-vein behavior presented as true for every member of the complex.
publicRows.classificationNote: Fungi form a separate kingdom. This row remains an actual biological subject, not a plant.

publicRows.label: Dead man's fingers (Xylaria polymorpha)
publicRows.notes: This fungus produces dark, finger-shaped reproductive structures on dead or dying wood. A rotting log now appears to be raising a corpse's hand. The forest has chosen deeply unsettling customer service.
verifiedFacts: Xylaria fruiting structures are finger-like and associated with dead or dying wood.
University of Georgia Extension identifies X. polymorpha by this common name.
removedClaims: Unsupported claim about routine cardiac events among field biologists.
publicRows.classificationNote: Fungi form a separate kingdom. This row remains an actual biological subject, not a plant.

publicRows.label: Sea cucumbers (Holothuroidea)
publicRows.notes: Some sea cucumbers expel internal organs when threatened and can regenerate the lost parts. Predator arrives; this animal rage-quits its own anatomy. Nature's most aggressive unboxing video.
verifiedFacts: Holothuroidea is a class containing many sea cucumber species.
Evisceration and subsequent regeneration occur in sea cucumbers; anatomy and timing differ by species.
removedClaims: Universal anal expulsion and fixed six-week regeneration deadline.
publicRows.classificationNote: This entry identifies a real class of animals, not a species or a documented individual.

publicRows.label: Tongue-replacing isopod (Cymothoa exigua)
publicRows.notes: This parasitic crustacean can cause a fish's tongue to degenerate and attach where it once sat. A roommate who takes the phrase 'shared kitchen' too literally.
verifiedFacts: The primary report documents tongue degeneration and attachment to the tongue stub and mouth floor in spotted rose snapper.
Functional mechanical replacement was proposed from observed feeding and anatomy.
removedClaims: False claim that the fish tastes through the parasite.
publicRows.sourceNote: Original research paper hosted by the Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum.

publicRows.label: Northern fulmar (Fulmarus glacialis)
publicRows.notes: Northern fulmars defend nesting sites by spitting foul-smelling stomach oil at intruders. Personal space, enforced with salad dressing.
verifiedFacts: Northern fulmars use oil-spitting to defend nesting sites.
The stomach oil is foul-smelling and is directed at threats.
removedClaims: Unsupported universal claim of permanent feather-waterproofing destruction.
publicRows.sourceNote: Animal Diversity Web is maintained by the University of Michigan Museum of Zoology.

publicRows.label: Hairy frog (Astylosternus robustus)
publicRows.notes: This frog can deploy sharp toe-bone claws through its skin when threatened. The emergency toolkit has no regard for the packaging.
verifiedFacts: AMNH currently places the hairy frog in Astylosternus; the prior Trichobatrachus combination refers to the same species.
The sharp phalanx separates from its anchoring nodule and pierces the skin.
removedClaims: Misleading claim that the frog snaps and splinters its own toe bones.
publicRows.classificationNote: Updated genus follows AMNH's current reference; historical names remain as aliases.

publicRows.label: Surinam toad (Pipa pipa)
publicRows.notes: Females carry developing young in pockets of skin on their backs; the offspring emerge as tiny, fully formed frogs. A family apartment building with extremely personal plumbing.
verifiedFacts: Eggs become embedded in the female's dorsal skin.
Young emerge as miniature frogs after development in these pockets.
publicRows.sourceNote: Animal Diversity Web is maintained by the University of Michigan Museum of Zoology.

privatePlan.label: Exploding ant (Colobopsis explodens)
privatePlan.notes: Small workers defend the colony by rupturing their bodies and releasing sticky gland secretions, killing themselves. A security system with no reset button.
verifiedFacts: Minor workers can rupture their bodies in defense.
The defending worker releases sticky gland secretions and dies.
privatePlan.mutationPlan: The owner-run SQL correction changes only the known Testing/testing... placeholder to this existing public specimen. Original rows are backed up before changes. No private row ids are invented.
